title: Alone in the field
hook: Rebbe Nachman of Breslov taught speaking to God in your own words, alone in nature

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking pilgrimage, and the psalm's line, our feet shall stand within thy gates. Your line was walking as prayer. Did an ordinary walk turn into a small pilgrimage? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

"And Isaac went out to meditate in the field at the eventide." One quiet sentence in Genesis, right before Isaac looks up and sees the camels bringing Rebekah. What was he doing out there, alone, at dusk? The Bible doesn't say. Jewish tradition has an answer: he was praying. Much later, a Hasidic teacher, Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, took that picture and made it a daily practice for anyone. Go out alone, he taught. Into a field if you can. And talk to God, not in the words of a prayer book, but in your own. These last days have been Christian ways of prayer. Today the path turns to Jewish ways, beginning in a field.
screen: `ISAAC IN THE FIELD AT DUSK.` → `TRADITION: HE WAS PRAYING.` → `GO OUT ALONE, AND TALK.`

segments.voice: Rebbe Nachman's word for it is hitbodedut, which means making yourself alone: seclusion, time set apart. Four turns. First, it's daily, and it's private. In his teachings, collected by his student Nathan, Nachman urges setting aside time every day to be alone, in a room or, better, out in the fields, and pour out your heart. He placed this practice very high among the ways of serving God. Second, your own language. Jewish prayer has its fixed services, in Hebrew, said at set times, and Nachman kept those. But hitbodedut is different. He says to speak in the language you actually speak, so the words come straight from the heart and you understand every one. Tell God everything, he says, the way you'd talk to a close friend: what went wrong today, what you want, what you're ashamed of, what you're afraid of. Third, when the words don't come. Nachman expected that. Some days, his teaching says, you'll sit there and nothing will come out. Then say even one word, over and over. Even just showing up and wanting to speak counts. Fourth, why a field. Nachman taught that when a person prays out among the grasses and plants, they join in the prayer, and lend it strength. The field isn't scenery. It's company. And Isaac? The rabbis of the Talmud read his walk in the field as prayer, and connect him with the afternoon prayer, mincha, said as the day turns toward evening. So a quiet line in Genesis becomes, in Breslov teaching, an invitation: go out, alone, and speak plainly.
screen: `DAILY, AND ALONE.` · `IN THE LANGUAGE YOU SPEAK.` · `WHEN NOTHING COMES, ONE WORD.` · `THE GRASSES JOIN IN.` · then, large: `AND ISAAC WENT OUT TO MEDITATE IN THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: speak your heart aloud, outdoors if you can. Step outside, or open a window, or just face one. Then talk, out loud, quietly, in your own everyday words. If you pray, speak to God the way you'd talk to a close friend: what's going on, what you need. If you don't, speak to the open air, or to someone you love, or simply say what's true for you today. If nothing comes, say one word, and say it again. The bell holds the time.
Hitbodedut. Seclusion: Rebbe Nachman's daily practice of going out alone, ideally into a field, and speaking to God in your own words. Today's word.

Your line: my own words. Today, find two minutes alone, a walk, a parked car, a back step, and say out loud, in plain words, one thing you haven't said to anyone. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Breslov Hasidim and others who practice hitbodedut set aside time each day, often outdoors or alone in a room, to speak to God aloud in their everyday language, alongside the fixed Jewish prayer services.

notes: Rebbe Nachman's teachings are paraphrased. Confirm: Likutei Moharan II:25 on daily hitbodedut, ideally in a field, in one's own spoken language, as with a friend, and its high place among ways of serving God; the 'even one word' teaching (possibly Likutei Moharan II:96 or Sichot HaRan; confirm the reference); II:11 on the grasses of the field joining in prayer.
No dates for Nachman given; the hook says only 'much later'.
Berakhot 26b links Isaac's 'lasuach' in the field (Genesis 24:63) to prayer and to mincha; paraphrased. Confirm.
Hitbodedut glossed as 'seclusion, making yourself alone' (meaning, not etymology); confirm Hebrew pointing and transliteration.
Turning point: first day of the 'Jewish ways' strand after Christian contemplative ways; the hook names the turn without comparing the two.
